title: The Day the Plans Went Wild
markdown:
The sea air smelled like adventure, a smell Imogen Quibble usually loved. Today it smelled a bit doom-y. It was the Seaside College Winter Fair, and for a junior reporter whose whiskers quivered for things to be just so, this was meant to be the crowning of her perfect plans. The Seaside College Chronicle wanted a report so shiny, so stuffed with quotes and pictures, that the editor’s glasses would fog. Her notebook — neat lines, colour-coded tabs — rode in her bag like a blueprint for amazing journalism.

“Okay,” she whispered, pushing up the round glasses that always slid. “Mrs. Higgins at the fancy cheese stall: a real quote, not just ‘it’s blue.’ Then The Barnacle Beats — last year’s sea songs, this year’s students still humming. Then the lighthouse against the evening sky. A picture so good it looks hired.” She paused, tasting a headline that would sing with holiday cheer.

A blustery, out-of-season gale arrived as if it had a grudge against tidy paper. Notes, pages, and a very silly flyer for the Most Glorious Beard contest — a side-event Imogen had wisely left out of her perfect report — swirled like a runaway confetti cannon.

“Oh, barnacles!” she squeaked, stoat paws scrambling for a page on photographing the candy-floss machine’s sugary swirl.

Caspar Wingate swooped in then, college photographer, a heron tall and grand with a beak that seemed to go on forever. He landed like a graceful, slightly clumsy laundry basket. Amber eyes took in the paper-storm. The flash on his camera glinted, a tiny sun ready to pop.

“Aha!” he boomed, foghorn clearing its throat, seagulls scattering. “What a pickle! Don’t you worry, young Quibble! Caspar’s here to lend a wing — or a beak!”

Before she could launch her polite-but-firm protest (honed on overly enthusiastic art students), Caspar began his help. He did not pick up papers so much as nudge them with that enormous beak into newer crazier directions. A flyer for the Coconut Shy of Calamity fetched up beside hot cross buns. Her perfectly drawn map of the fair went, with a pleased little shove, into a shimmering puddle from the morning’s unexpected rain.

“There!” He puffed glossy chest feathers. “Much tidier. Now — the cheese!” He took a bunch of pictures of Imogen clutching her slightly damp notebook, looking completely baffled.

Annoyance bubbled. Strangely, a laugh sat under it. His help was disastrous and he was so ridiculously sure of himself that anger could not quite land. “Caspar,” she tried, calm as a lake, “my plan was actually very precise—”

“Plans are for the birds, my dear!” His rumbling laugh tickled her whiskers. Wide wings sent a note about a Gnome-Painting Workshop fluttering onto Professor Fitzwilliam, a man of big brain and bigger eyebrows. “We need excitement! The thrill of the moment!”

That moment became a series of wonderfully weird events, all Caspar’s well-intentioned mess. He saw a child lighting a tiny lantern and, with a confident flick, struck a match. Too much enthusiasm: a whole string of fairy lights caught and tumbled, a festive fantastically tangled sparkle over the hot-chocolate queue.

Bored students waited for drinks. Caspar, convinced they were admiring his photography, struck dramatic poses. Spindly legs made a dance-like shape against the busy fair.

Imogen did her own frantic dance, catching each fix before it became a complete disaster. She rescued the soggy map, now wearing a clear beak-print. She told Professor Fitzwilliam the fluttering note was not a message from the universe, only a keen heron. She even got a few sensible sentences about the mild flavour of the Gorgonzola before Caspar, deciding the stall needed oomph, perched on its awning. A small memorable cheese avalanche followed.

She watched a perfectly good wheel of Stilton perform a dramatic roll into discarded raffle tickets, and did not bother announcing that this was the opposite of her plan. The wheel made its own argument.

Caspar, unbothered, organised the Ferris wheel queue into what he believed was a harmonious bird-like pattern. The result looked less like a queue than a confused flock of sheep. Imogen found herself explaining to a young man Caspar had guided into a thorny rose bush. She could explain everything except why it now looked like a deliberately messy art project.

Afternoon wore on. The fair was nothing like the colour-coded notebook. Gingerbread men wore funny ink-smudged moustaches. Carol singers, in accidental genius, swapped songs with a heartfelt speech about physics. The raffle’s knitted scarf ended in the nest of a very possessive seagull.

Imogen slumped against a lamppost, a flat balloon of journalistic despair. Notebook soggy. Gorgonzola scoop sunk. Heart, traitorously, rather full. Caspar, creating exciting lighting for the college choir by flapping at the setting sun, made the singers look as if they had joined a wild disco.

Then she noticed. Students, teachers, townspeople who had braved the wind — they were not scowling. They were laughing. Pointing. Talking, faces lit with real fun. The accidental glitter at the craft stall. The catchy singing of science formulas. The cheese avalanche that somehow made people share. Charming, in the way a wave is charming after it has soaked your shoes.

A young woman, cheeks pink from the wind, caught Imogen’s eye and gestured at the scene. “Isn’t it just wonderful? So much more alive than if everything had gone perfectly.”

Imogen looked, really looked. Bikes parked nearby, shiny parts gleaming like a promise of fun after rain. Families huddled in a big laugh. Students, earlier gloom forgotten, untangling the now-sparkling fairy lights. And Caspar, perched on the lighthouse like a king, as the beam swept its grand arc across the choppy grey sea.

He swooped down, a rustle of feathers. “Well?” Less foghorn now, more waves. “A triumph, wouldn’t you say?”

Imogen smiled, a real one that reached her whiskers. “Yes, Caspar. Yes, I suppose it was.”

The gale eased. The lighthouse kept writing its pale circle on the water. Imogen tucked the beak-printed map into the soggy notebook and did not try to flatten either of them. Somewhere, a seagull guarded a scarf, and the hot-chocolate queue glittered as if it had meant to all along.
characters: Imogen (a stoat junior reporter), Caspar (the heron photographer)
audience: young adults aged 16-18, teen anthology entry
author: StoryGen Community
